title: Chapter 19
paragraphs: When Anna walked into the room, Dolly was sitting in the little drawing-room with a fair-haired, plump little boy who was already like his father, giving him a lesson in French reading. As the boy read, he kept fidgeting and trying to tear off a button that was nearly off his jacket. His mother had taken his hand away from it several times, but the plump little hand kept going back to the button. His mother pulled the button off and put it in her pocket.

"Keep your hands still, Grisha," she said, and she took up her work, a coverlet she had been making for a long time. She always took it up at depressing moments, and now she was knitting at it nervously, fingers twitching, counting the stitches. Although she had sent word the day before to her husband that it was nothing to her whether his sister came or not, she had made everything ready for her arrival and was waiting for her sister-in-law with emotion.

Dolly was crushed by her sorrow, completely swallowed up by it. Still, she did not forget that Anna, her sister-in-law, was the wife of one of the most important people in Petersburg and a Petersburg _grande dame_. And thanks to this circumstance she did not carry out her threat to her husband — that is, she remembered that her sister-in-law was coming. "And, after all, Anna isn't in any way to blame," Dolly thought. "I know nothing but the very best of her, and I've seen nothing but kindness and affection from her toward myself." It was true that, as far as she could recall her impressions in Petersburg at the Karenins', she had not liked their household itself; there had been something artificial about the whole framework of their family life. "But why shouldn't I receive her? Only let her not take it into her head to console me!" Dolly thought. "All those consolations and counsels and Christian forgivenesses — I've thought them all over a thousand times, and they're no use."

All these days Dolly had been alone with the children. She did not want to talk about her sorrow, but with that sorrow in her heart she could not talk about anything outside it. She knew that one way or another she would tell Anna everything, and she was alternately glad at the thought of speaking freely and angry at the necessity of speaking of her humiliation to her, his sister, and of hearing her ready-made phrases of advice and comfort. She had been on the watch for her, glancing at her watch every minute, and, as so often happens, she missed the very minute her visitor arrived, so that she did not hear the bell.
Hearing a rustle of skirts and light steps at the door, she looked around, and her care-worn face involuntarily expressed not gladness but astonishment. She got up and embraced her sister-in-law.
"What, here already?" she said as she kissed her.
"Dolly, how glad I am to see you!"

"I'm glad too," said Dolly, smiling faintly, trying from the expression on Anna's face to make out whether she knew. "Most likely she knows," she thought, noticing the sympathy on Anna's face. "Well, come along, I'll take you to your room," she went on, trying to put off the moment of confidences as long as possible.
"Is this Grisha? Heavens, how he's grown!" said Anna; and kissing him, her eyes never leaving Dolly's, she stood there and flushed a little. "No, please, let's stay here."
She took off her kerchief and hat, snagging the hat on a lock of her thick black curls, then tossed her head and shook her hair loose.
"You're radiant with health and happiness!" Dolly said, almost with envy.

"I?... Yes," said Anna. "Merciful heavens, Tanya! You're the same age as my Seryozha," she added, turning to the little girl as she ran in. She took her in her arms and kissed her. "Delightful child, delightful! Show me them all."
She named them — remembering not just their names but their ages, months, characters, and illnesses — and Dolly could not help being touched by it.
"Very well, we'll go to them," she said. "It's a pity Vassya is asleep."
After seeing the children, they sat down together over coffee in the drawing-room, alone now. Anna took the tray, and then pushed it away from her.
"Dolly," she said, "he's told me."
Dolly looked coldly at Anna; she was waiting now for the conventional phrases of sympathy, but Anna said nothing of the kind.
"Dolly, dear," she said, "I don't want to speak for him to you, or to try to console you — that can't be done. But, darling, I am simply sorry — sorry from my heart for you."

Under the thick lashes of her shining eyes, tears suddenly glittered. She moved closer to her sister-in-law and took her hand in her firm little one. Dolly did not pull away, but her face did not lose its frigid expression. She said:
"To comfort me is impossible. Everything is lost after what has happened, everything is over!"
And the moment she had said this, her face suddenly softened. Anna lifted Dolly's wasted, thin hand, kissed it, and said:
"But, Dolly, what's to be done, what's to be done? How is it best to act in this awful position — that's what you have to think about."

"All's over, and there's nothing more," Dolly said. "And the worst of it, you see, is that I can't simply throw him off — there are the children, I'm bound. And I can't live with him; it's a torture for me to see him."
"Dolly, darling, he's spoken to me, but I want to hear it from you: tell me about it."
Dolly looked at her questioningly.
Sympathy and unfeigned love showed on Anna's face.

"Very well," she said all at once. "But I'll tell it from the beginning. You know how I was married. With the upbringing mamma gave us I was more than innocent, I was stupid. I knew nothing. They say men tell their wives about their former lives, but Stiva" — she corrected herself — "Stepan Arkadyevitch told me nothing. You'll hardly believe it, but until now I imagined that I was the only woman he had ever known. That's how I lived for eight years. You have to understand that I was so far from suspecting infidelity that I regarded it as impossible, and then — try to imagine it — with such ideas, suddenly to find out all the horror, all the loathsomeness... You have to try to understand me. To be completely convinced of one's happiness, and all at once..." Dolly went on, holding back her sobs, "to get a letter — his letter to his mistress, my governess. No, it's too awful!" She quickly pulled out her handkerchief and hid her face in it. "I can understand being carried away by feeling," she went on after a brief silence, "but to deceive me deliberately, slyly... and with whom? To go on being my husband together with her... it's awful! You can't understand..."
"Oh yes, I understand! I understand! Dolly, dearest, I do understand," said Anna, pressing her hand.
"And do you imagine he realizes the full awfulness of my position?" Dolly went on. "Not in the slightest! He's happy and content."
"Oh, no!" Anna broke in quickly. "He's to be pitied — he's weighed down by remorse..."
"Is he capable of remorse?" Dolly cut in, gazing intently into her sister-in-law's face.

"Yes. I know him. I couldn't look at him without feeling sorry for him. We both know him. He's good-hearted, but he's proud, and now he's so humiliated. What touched me most..." (and here Anna guessed what would touch Dolly most) "he's tortured by two things: that he's ashamed for the children's sake, and that, loving you — yes, yes, loving you beyond everything on earth," she hurriedly cut off Dolly, who would have answered — "he has hurt you, pierced you to the heart. 'No, no, she cannot forgive me,' he keeps saying."
Dolly looked dreamily away past her sister-in-law as she listened.

"Yes, I can see that his position is awful — it's worse for the guilty than the innocent," she said, "if he feels that all the misery comes from his own fault. But how am I to forgive him, how am I to be his wife again after her? For me to live with him now would be torture, just because I love what I used to feel for him..."
And sobs cut off her words. But as if on purpose, each time she softened she began again to talk about what made her furious.

"She's young, you see, she's pretty," she went on. "Do you know, Anna, my youth and my looks are gone, taken by whom? By him and his children. I've worked for him, and everything I had has gone in his service, and now of course any fresh, vulgar creature has more charm for him. No doubt they talked about me together, or, worse, were silent. Do you understand?"
Again her eyes burned with hatred.

"And after all that he will tell me... What? Can I believe him? Never! No, everything is over, everything that was once my comfort, the reward for my work and my suffering... Would you believe it, I was teaching Grisha just now: once this was a joy to me, now it's a torture. What do I have to strive and toil for? Why are the children here? What's so awful is that all at once my heart has turned, and instead of love and tenderness I have nothing but hatred for him; yes, hatred. I could kill him."
"Darling Dolly, I understand, but don't torture yourself. You're so distressed, so overwrought, that you're seeing many things wrongly."
Dolly grew calmer, and for two minutes both were silent.
"What's to be done? Think for me, Anna, help me. I've thought it all over and I can see nothing."
Anna could think of nothing, but her heart responded instantly to every word, every change of expression on her sister-in-law's face.

"There's one thing I would say," Anna began. "I'm his sister, I know his character — that capacity for forgetting everything, everything" (she waved her hand before her forehead), "that capacity for being completely carried away, but also for completely repenting. He can't believe it, he can't understand now how he could have acted as he did."
"No; he understands, he understood!" Dolly cut in. "But I... you're forgetting me... does it make it any easier for me?"

"Wait a minute. When he told me, I'll admit, I didn't realize the full awfulness of your position. I saw only him, and that the family was broken up. I felt sorry for him, but after talking to you I see it, as a woman, quite differently. I see your agony, and I can't tell you how sorry I am for you. But, Dolly, darling, while I fully realize your suffering, there is one thing I don't know: I don't know... I don't know how much love there still is in your heart for him. You know that — whether there is enough for you to be able to forgive him. If there is, forgive him!"
"No," Dolly was beginning, but Anna cut her short, kissing her hand again.

"I know more of the world than you do," she said. "I know how men like Stiva see it. You said he talks about you with her. That never happened. Such men are unfaithful, but their home and their wife are sacred to them. Somehow these women are still looked on by them with contempt, and don't touch their feeling for their family. They draw a kind of line that can't be crossed between them and their families. I don't understand it, but it is so."
"Yes, but he has kissed her..."

"Dolly, hush, darling. I saw Stiva when he was in love with you. I remember the time when he came to me and cried, talking about you, and all the poetry and the loftiness of his feelings for you, and I know that the longer he lived with you the loftier you stood in his eyes. You know we used to laugh at him for putting in at every word, 'Dolly is a marvelous woman.' You've always been a divinity to him, and you are that still, and this hasn't been an infidelity of the heart..."
"But if it's repeated?"
"It can't be, as I see it..."
"Yes, but could you forgive it?"

"I don't know, I can't judge... Yes, I can," Anna said, thinking for a moment; and, grasping the situation in her thoughts and weighing it in her inner balance, she added, "Yes, I can, I can, I can. Yes, I could forgive it. I couldn't be the same, no; but I could forgive it, and forgive it as though it had never been, never been at all..."

"Oh, of course," Dolly broke in quickly, as if saying what she had thought more than once. "Otherwise it wouldn't be forgiveness. If one forgives, it has to be completely, completely. Come, let's go; I'll take you to your room," she said, getting up, and on the way she embraced Anna. "My dear, how glad I am you came. It has made things better, ever so much better."
